newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks end flat after seesaw session.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks end flat after seesaw session.

text.p: Tokyo stocks ended flat on Friday after the market benchmark wandered in both negative and positive ranges for most of the day.

"Thursday's property-related share rally spilled over into the Friday session while a stronger yen prompted profit-taking of export-strong blue-chip shares, forcing the Nikkei average to seesaw around the 19,000 level," said Akihiro Naemura, general manager at Okasan Securities.
The Nikkei 225 clawed back above the 19,000 line to close down 17.17 points or 0.09 percent at 19,034.54. Its March futures were down 40 points at 19,030.
Brokers said the Nikkei 225 and its futures were weighed down by selling of recent high flyers such as Sony Corp, which shed 140 yen to end at 8,750.

But the TOPIX index, encompassing banking, construction and other sectors groaning under bad loans, kept climbing, still nourished by newspaper reports on Thursday that the government may use public funds to buy land formerly owned by failed housing loan firms and other troubled financial institutions.
The TOPIX rose 13.35 points or 0.95 percent to end at 1,425.01. The Nikkei 300 added 2.97 points or 1.10 percent to close at 273.90.
The second section index climbed 1.44 points or 0.08 percent to 1,731.67.

Media reports that the government may ease regulations on building ratios in big cities to increase the number of high-rise apartment blocks also lent support to property-related shares, said Yasuo Ueki, Nikko Securities general manager.

The Nihon Keizai Shimbun reported that the Construction Ministry was proposing a doubling of the current ratio of 400 percent and also to abolish zoning laws which prevent buildings from obstructing sunlight.

Winners pulled ahead of losers by 614 to 507 issues, while 140 issues were unchanged. First-section turnover was 596 million shares, down a tad from 613 million on Thursday. A total 7.82 million second-section shares changed hands compared with 8.88 million the previous day.
Brokers said the Nikkei average would make efforts next week to secure a foothold above the 19,000 line.
"The benchmark has reached a stage where it is getting close to retracing one-third of its worth from the January 10 low of 17,303 and the high of 22,666 marked on June 26," Okasan's Naemura said.
"Consolidation at the one-third retracement level is needed before further rises can be achieved," he added.
But despite the somewhat optimistic mood, some market sources said buying was still cautious and was centred on buy-backs.

"Just how much can be bought back remains to be seen," a broker at a second-tier brokerage said. "Further strengthening of the yen could fuel profit-taking of exporters, and if buying of domestic issues and blue-chips peter out at once, market senitment could sour."
Leading machine tool manufacturer Okuma Corp tumbled on a ratings cut, shedding 130 yen to 1,010, the largest percentage loser on the first section of the bourse.

Sharp Corp fell on media reports, later confirmed by the company, that its parent current profit for the year to March 31 was likely to fall 2.0 billion yen short of its previous forecast. It lost 60 yen to 1,530 by the day's end.
Contractor Kumagai Gumi led the construction sector, rising 14 yen to 203 yen in a trade of 5.434 million shares, the most actively traded issue on the first section of the Tokyo bourse.

By sector, real estate, banks, securities, construction and insurance issues were the main gainers. The decliners were headed by transport equipment, fisheries, ceramics, gas and electrical equipment.
The over-the-counter index was down 4.52 points or 0.37 percent at 1,212.62.
--Masako Iijima, Tokyo Equities Desk (+81-3-3432-9052)
